name: remove.bg
title: PrivaTools vs remove.bg: what changes on 1 December 2026
description: remove.bg's website closes on 1 December 2026 as background removal moves to Canva. Its credits, limits and API compared with PrivaTools' free remover.
summary: remove.bg says its standalone website will no longer be available from 1 December 2026 at 9:00am CET: background removal moves to Canva, API access moves to Leonardo.ai and unused pay-as-you-go credits expire that day. Until then it offers free previews up to 0.25 megapixels and paid credits for full resolution. PrivaTools' Background Remover is free at the image's original size, with a server engine or an on-device model.
highlights: remove.bg's website and accounts close on 1 December 2026.
Full resolution costs a credit per image there; PrivaTools is free at full size.
An on-device engine option, against processing only on remove.bg's servers.
overview: remove.bg removes image backgrounds with AI through its website, an API, desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux, an Android app and plugins such as one for Photoshop. A notice across its site says background removal is moving to Canva, and its FAQ says the standalone website, accounts and self-service API end on 1 December 2026 at 9:00am CET, with API access moving to Leonardo.ai, which its API page describes as also part of Canva.

Until that date, previews on the website are free up to 0.25 megapixels for personal use, and each full-resolution image costs one credit, bought in pay-as-you-go packs or a monthly subscription. Uploads can be JPG, PNG or WebP files up to 22 MB and 50 megapixels. Its help centre says the uploaded image and the result are deleted about an hour after upload at the latest, and API images right after the call.

features.label: Price
features.privatools: Free at the image's original size, with no credits to buy.
features.competitor: Website previews are free; each full-resolution image costs 1 credit, from packs or a subscription.

features.label: Use of results
features.privatools: The terms leave all rights to your files and outputs with you.
features.competitor: Free use and use without an account are for non-commercial purposes only.

features.label: File limits
features.privatools: JPG, PNG or WebP. The in-browser engine takes images up to 40 megapixels; the server engine takes files of about 250 MB.
features.competitor: JPG, PNG or WebP up to 22 MB and 50 megapixels; previews are capped at 0.25 megapixels.

features.label: Where images are processed
features.privatools: On PrivaTools' server by default, or in your browser with the downloaded U-2-Net model.
features.competitor: On its servers. Its desktop app also sends images to the remove.bg API and needs an internet connection.

features.label: Retention
features.privatools: Temporary files are removed after the response, and a sweep clears leftovers older than ten minutes.
features.competitor: Upload and result deleted about an hour after upload at the latest; API images right after the call.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed for the tool or its batch download.
features.competitor: Not needed for website previews; generating an API key requires an account.

features.label: API
features.privatools: Background removal is one of the operations in the free, key-authenticated PrivaTools API.
features.competitor: The first 50 API calls a month are free; from 1 December 2026 background removal moves to Leonardo.ai.

features.label: What happens next
features.privatools: The tool is part of the open-source PrivaTools codebase and can also be self-hosted.
features.competitor: Website, accounts, self-service API and plugins end on 1 December 2026; unused pay-as-you-go credits expire.

sections.heading: What 1 December 2026 changes
body: remove.bg's FAQ sets out the closure. From 1 December 2026 at 9:00am CET the website and accounts will not be accessible, the self-service API stops accepting requests, unused pay-as-you-go credits expire, and the Photoshop plugin and other integrations are discontinued. A subscription ends automatically, and any final renewal on or after 1 November is free. The FAQ says Canva's background remover uses the same technology.

If you still hold credits, download the full-resolution results you need before that date. A workflow built on the remove.bg API or a plugin needs a new home: Leonardo.ai for the API, according to remove.bg, or another tool.

sections.heading: Replacing it with PrivaTools
body: PrivaTools' Background Remover returns a transparent PNG at the original dimensions, without an account, credits or a personal-use restriction. Its default server engine runs the compact U-2-Net model, u2netp, on the PrivaTools server. The in-browser engine downloads the same model, about 4.4 MB plus its runtime, and then processes images on your device, so they are not uploaded for that path.

remove.bg says its algorithms are trained to handle hard elements such as hair, and it adds background generation and bulk editing. PrivaTools only produces the cut-out, and u2netp is a small model: hair, fur, glass and motion blur can come out rough. We have not compared the two services, so test your hardest images before you move a product catalogue.

chooseCompetitor: You have remove.bg credits or a subscription to use before 1 December 2026.
You design in Canva, which is where remove.bg says its background removal is going.
You need 50-megapixel output, AI-generated backgrounds or its bulk editing before the closure.
choosePrivaTools: You need transparent PNGs after 1 December 2026 without a Canva account.
You want full-size cut-outs without buying credits or accepting a non-commercial limit.
You want the choice to keep images on your device with the in-browser engine.
You want background removal through a free API key you can call from your own scripts.
tradeoffs: remove.bg's help centre says uploads are not used to train its AI, while its privacy policy says account content may be analysed to train its models; read both if that matters to you.
PrivaTools' model is compact, which suits quick cut-outs; inspect edges on dark and light backgrounds before relying on a result.
Neither service's output quality was benchmarked for this page.

name: iLovePDF
title: PrivaTools vs iLovePDF: free limits, apps and file handling
description: iLovePDF's free Basic plan caps files per task and size, and Premium adds desktop and mobile apps. PrivaTools is free with open code. Limits compared.
summary: iLovePDF is a broad PDF suite on the web, Windows, macOS, iOS and Android. Its free Basic plan works without an account but limits files per task and file size, and Premium unlocks the desktop and mobile apps, workflows, digital signatures and much larger files. PrivaTools has no paid plan, adds image, media and developer tools and publishes its code, but it has no native apps.
highlights: Free merging: 25 files and 100 MB on iLovePDF Basic, 100 files and 500 MB on PrivaTools.
Desktop and mobile apps come with Premium; PrivaTools runs in the browser.
Files deleted within two hours there, against cleanup after each response.
overview: iLovePDF, from ILOVEPDF S.L. in Barcelona, offers PDF tools on the web, desktop apps for Windows and macOS, iOS and Android apps and a Chrome extension. Its free Basic plan covers the essential tools with limited processing and needs no account, although its AI tools require one. Premium, for up to 25 users, adds every tool, unlimited processing, desktop and mobile access, workflows, digital signatures, an ad-free experience and 2,000 AI credits a month.

Files uploaded to the web service are processed on iLovePDF's servers and deleted automatically within two hours. Premium and Business users can choose the region where files are processed, and the desktop app processes files on your computer. Its developer product, iLoveAPI, offers PDF, image and signature tools as a REST API with a monthly allowance of free credits.

features.label: Price
features.privatools: Every tool is free; there is no Premium tier to unlock.
features.competitor: Basic is free; Premium is billed monthly or yearly for up to 25 users; Business pricing is quoted.

features.label: Free-plan limits
features.privatools: No task quota on the website; heavy jobs such as OCR allow five runs a minute per IP.
features.competitor: Basic processes a limited number of documents, and tools such as OCR to Word and PDF/A are Premium only.

features.label: Files and size
features.privatools: Merge takes up to 100 PDFs in one 500 MB request; most single-file pages take about 250 MB.
features.competitor: Basic merges 25 files up to 100 MB; Office conversion and OCR take one 15 MB file; Premium goes to 4 GB.

features.label: Where files are processed
features.privatools: Most PDF tools run on the PrivaTools server in temporary per-request storage; text and developer tools run in your browser.
features.competitor: On its servers; Premium and Business users can choose the region where files are processed.

features.label: Retention
features.privatools: Response cleanup removes each job's files; a sweep clears leftovers after ten minutes.
features.competitor: Files are deleted automatically within two hours of processing on its servers.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed for any tool; an optional account issues API keys.
features.competitor: Not needed for the free web tools; its AI tools require a user account.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Any modern browser, installable as a web app; no native apps.
features.competitor: Web, Windows 10 or later, macOS 12 or later, iOS and Android apps.

features.label: API
features.privatools: A free key with a default daily allowance of 500 processing units.
features.competitor: iLoveAPI gives 2,500 free credits a month on registration, with paid credit plans in US dollars.

sections.heading: Reading the Basic plan
body: iLovePDF sets its free limits per tool rather than per day. On Basic, merging takes up to 25 files and 100 MB, compression takes two files up to 200 MB, and Office conversion and OCR take one file of 15 MB, while editing and splitting take one file on every plan. Some tools, including OCR conversion to Word or Excel and PDF/A, are marked as not included in Basic. The pricing table is not fully consistent: it lists Basic limits for a few tools it also marks as Premium only.

PrivaTools uses one set of limits for everyone: 500 MB per upload request, about 250 MB per file on most single-file pages, up to 25 files queued on a standard tool page, and up to 100 PDFs in one merge. There is no Premium to lift them on the public site, although a self-hosted copy can raise the request cap.

sections.heading: Apps, regions and signatures
body: Premium includes iLovePDF's desktop apps, which process files on your computer, and its mobile apps. Premium users can pick among seven processing regions and Business users among eleven. Its signature tool embeds a certified hash and qualified timestamp, and its security page says signed documents are kept for up to five years to meet legal requirements.

PrivaTools has no native apps and no region choice on the public site; if location or offline processing matters, you can run it on your own hardware. Its Sign PDF and E-Sign PDF place a visible signature image and do not create certificate-based or certified signatures.

chooseCompetitor: You want native desktop and mobile apps under one PDF subscription.
You send documents for signature and want its certified signatures with a qualified timestamp.
You need files processed in a specific region, or files far larger than PrivaTools accepts.
Your files live in Google Drive or Dropbox, which it integrates with.
choosePrivaTools: You want free use without per-tool file-count tiers or a sign-up.
You want source code you can inspect and a copy you can host.
You also work with images, audio, video, archives or developer formats.
tradeoffs: iLovePDF showed us its prices in Indian rupees, based on our location, so this page quotes no figure; check the pricing page from where you are.
Its security page and business page cite different versions of its ISO 27001 certification; check the current certificate if procurement depends on it.
We did not benchmark conversion quality or speed for either product.

name: Smallpdf
title: PrivaTools vs Smallpdf: free downloads, Pro and Sign.com
description: Smallpdf's free plan limits daily downloads and AI use, and Pro bundles Sign.com and a Windows app. PrivaTools is free with open code. Plans and data compared.
summary: Smallpdf offers PDF tools on the web, free iOS and Android apps with more for Pro users, a Windows desktop app and a Chrome extension and apps for Google Workspace and Dropbox. Its free plan works without signing up for most tools but limits downloads, compression strength and AI use; Pro lifts those limits and includes Sign.com e-signatures, and first-time subscribers can take a 7-day trial that asks for payment details. PrivaTools is free throughout and open source, with no native apps.
highlights: Daily download limits on Smallpdf's free plan, against no task quota.
Pro includes Sign.com signature requests; PrivaTools places signature images only.
Processing on EU servers, against temporary processing you can also self-host.
overview: Smallpdf's pricing page lists Free, Pro, Team and Business plans. The free plan offers limited document downloads, limited mobile app access and a Sign.com account limited to two documents a month; Pro adds unlimited downloads, text editing, OCR, strong compression, unlimited AI tools and unlimited mobile access. Its Windows desktop app handles files offline, and its macOS app has not been supported since October 2021.

Uploaded files are processed on Hetzner servers in the European Union. With a user account, files are deleted within one hour unless you save them to your storage; the support page says files are removed an hour after processing for most tools. AI features use OpenAI, and Smallpdf says it does not share your content with OpenAI for training. It states that it is ISO/IEC 27001 certified.

features.privatools: Free throughout; nothing to subscribe to.
features.competitor: Free plan; Pro billed monthly or yearly; Team and Business plans; a 7-day Pro trial.

features.label: Free-plan limits
features.privatools: No daily allowance; heavy jobs allow five runs a minute per IP.
features.competitor: Most tools carry a daily download limit; AI tools allow up to 4 documents a day.

features.privatools: 500 MB per upload request; about 250 MB per file on most single-file pages.
features.competitor: The free file size is marked Limited without a number, paid plans Unlimited; AI files up to 50 MB.

features.privatools: In your browser or in PrivaTools' temporary server storage, as each tool states.
features.competitor: On Hetzner servers in the European Union.

features.privatools: Cleaned after the response, with a sweep for leftovers older than ten minutes.
features.competitor: For most tools, files are removed from its servers an hour after processing.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed for any tool.
features.competitor: Most tools can be tried without signing up, with some limitations.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Browser on any operating system; installable as a web app.
features.competitor: Web and a Windows desktop app that works offline; its macOS app is marked unsupported.

features.label: Signatures
features.privatools: Sign PDF and E-Sign PDF place a drawn, typed or uploaded signature image.
features.competitor: Sign.com can request signatures, track activity, add digital seals and issue a certificate of completion.

sections.heading: What the free plan leaves out
body: Smallpdf meters its free plan by day. Most tools carry a daily download limit, the mobile apps a daily task limit, and strong compression, batch processing, OCR to Office formats, text editing and image extraction are Pro features. The support page mentions two conversions a day, while the pricing page gives no single daily number.

PrivaTools does not meter use by day. Its Extreme compression preset, batch queues of up to 25 files, OCR and PDF to Word are all available without an account, within the request size limit and per-IP rate limits on heavy jobs. It has no mode for editing existing PDF text, paid or free: Edit PDF adds new content on top of the page.

sections.heading: Signing and AI
body: Pro bundles Sign.com, so one subscription covers editing and signature requests with tracking and a certificate of completion. Smallpdf's AI tools, including chat with PDF, summaries and translation, are part of its plans. PrivaTools' AI tools need either an on-device model download or your own provider key, and its signature tools place an image rather than running a signing workflow.
If most of your work is sending contracts for signature, Smallpdf with Sign.com covers more of it. If you mostly compress, convert and tidy documents, PrivaTools covers that without a plan.

chooseCompetitor: You want mobile apps and a Windows app alongside the website under one subscription.
You collect signatures from other people and need tracking and a certificate of completion.
You want AI chat, summaries and translation included without supplying your own AI key.
Your documents already live in Google Workspace or Dropbox.
choosePrivaTools: You need more than a few downloads a day without paying.
You want strong compression, OCR or batch runs without a subscription.
You prefer open code, or to host the service yourself.
tradeoffs: Smallpdf's own pages give different figures for its tool count, yearly discount and team size; rely on the pricing page for the plan you choose.
Its privacy notice describes different deletion rules with and without an account; check which applies before uploading sensitive files.
We did not benchmark output quality or speed.

name: Adobe Acrobat
title: PrivaTools vs Adobe Acrobat: plans, free tools and editing
description: Adobe Acrobat's free online tools allow one task without signing in, and text editing needs a paid plan; PrivaTools is free with no account. Plans compared.
summary: Adobe Acrobat spans free Acrobat Reader, free online tools with trial limits, and paid Standard, Pro and Studio plans that add editing of existing text, signature requests, redaction, comparison and AI. PrivaTools is free and needs no account for any tool, and covers media and developer tasks too, but it cannot edit existing PDF text or run signature workflows, and it has no desktop app.
highlights: One free online task without signing in, against no task quota and no sign-in.
Existing-text editing on paid plans, which PrivaTools does not offer.
Certificate signatures and signature requests, against image signatures only.
overview: Adobe Acrobat comes as free Acrobat Reader, free online tools and subscription plans: Acrobat Express, Standard, Pro and Studio, each with a team version. Editing text and images requires Standard or Pro, not Reader. Standard adds signature requests with tracking; Pro adds version comparison, redaction, bulk e-signature requests and OCR; Studio includes everything in Pro plus PDF Spaces, AI Assistant for Acrobat and Adobe Express Premium.

Acrobat's online services upload files to Adobe cloud storage and protect them with AES-256 encryption and TLS 1.2. Without signing in, most online tools allow one free task and one download, and Adobe deletes the file from its servers soon afterwards. The desktop apps run on Windows and macOS, and Adobe says it does not use your documents or data to train AI models.

features.label: Price
features.privatools: Free, with no subscription, trial or licence.
features.competitor: In the US: Standard US$14.99, Pro US$19.99 and Studio US$24.99 a month on an annual plan billed monthly.

features.label: Free online limits
features.privatools: No task quota; heavy jobs allow five runs a minute per IP.
features.competitor: Without signing in, most tools allow one free task and one download; signed-in users get a premium task every 30 days.

features.label: File limits
features.privatools: 500 MB per request, Merge up to 100 PDFs, about 250 MB per file on most pages.
features.competitor: Online tools take PDFs up to 100 MB, PDF to Word and PowerPoint 200 MB and Compress 2 GB; Merge takes 100 files.

features.label: Where files are processed
features.privatools: No cloud library: server tools work on temporary copies, and browser-only tools process on your device.
features.competitor: Online tools upload to Adobe cloud storage, in data centres in North America, EMEA and Japan.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed for any tool.
features.competitor: A few online tools need sign-in, and saving or sharing a result needs an Adobe ID.

features.label: Editing existing text
features.privatools: Not available: Edit PDF adds text, drawings, images and whiteout on top of the page.
features.competitor: Needs a Standard or Pro subscription; Acrobat Reader cannot edit text or images.

features.label: Signatures
features.privatools: Places visible signature images and checks existing signatures against the file, but cannot sign with a certificate.
features.competitor: Acrobat and Acrobat Reader sign PDFs with certificate signatures and validate signed files.

features.label: Source code
features.privatools: MIT-licensed and self-hostable.
features.competitor: Licensed, not sold; the terms forbid attempts to discover the source code.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Any modern browser, including on Linux; installable as a web app.
features.competitor: Desktop apps for 64-bit Windows 10 and 11 and for macOS 13 or later.

sections.heading: Free tools or a subscription
body: Adobe's free online tools work as a trial of the paid product. Without an Adobe ID, most tools allow one task and one download; with one, you can share, fill, sign and comment on PDFs free, and try premium tools once every 30 days. Removing a password needs a subscription or the seven-day Acrobat Pro trial, and Adobe notes that a password added with the free Protect PDF tool cannot then be removed with it. Page tools such as rotate and extract handle up to 1,500 pages.
PrivaTools has no trial logic. Protect PDF, Unlock PDF, compression, conversion, OCR and redaction are free on every run, within the request size and rate limits, and nothing requires signing in.

sections.heading: Where Acrobat does more
body: Acrobat edits existing text and images and adjusts the formatting, compares versions, creates web forms and reusable e-sign templates, repairs accessibility tagging in Pro and saves PDF/A, PDF/X and PDF/E files in Pro. It signs with certificates and validates signed files, and Standard and above request signatures and track responses. Its AI Assistant, included in Studio or added to other plans, processes documents in Adobe's cloud with Microsoft Azure OpenAI.

PrivaTools covers parts of this with separate free tools: Compare PDF shows visual or text differences, Form Creator adds fillable fields, the Accessibility Checker audits tagging without changing the file, Redact PDF removes the content under each box, and Verify Digital Signature checks whether each signature still matches the file, without checking the certificate against a trust list. It has no text editing and no certificate signing, and its AI tools use on-device models or your own provider key.

chooseCompetitor: You edit existing text and images in PDFs as part of daily work.
You need certificate-based signatures, or signature requests with tracking.
You produce PDF/A files or repair accessibility tagging with Acrobat Pro.
Your team needs licences managed centrally across desktop, web and mobile.
choosePrivaTools: You need a task done in a browser without an Adobe ID or a trial.
You protect, unlock, compress, convert, OCR or redact files often and want that free.
You want open code you can host yourself, on any operating system.
tradeoffs: Adobe's pages list plans and AI add-ons differently: the US pricing page shows Acrobat Express and a US$1.99 AI Assistant add-on, while the trial page offers AI Assistant Plus at US$4.99. Check the plan page for your country.
The online-tool limits here come from an Adobe help article last updated in June 2025, the newest we found.
We did not benchmark either product's output.

name: Sejda PDF
title: PrivaTools vs Sejda PDF: free limits, pricing and Desktop
description: Sejda PDF limits free use to three tasks an hour and sells Web and Desktop passes; PrivaTools has no task quota. Limits, data paths and tools compared.
summary: Sejda PDF is a mature PDF toolset with a web version and a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux. Its free tier is capped per document and per hour, and paid passes remove those caps. PrivaTools has no task quota or paid tier and adds image, media and developer tools, but its editor adds content on top of pages rather than editing the existing text, which Sejda offers.
highlights: Three free tasks an hour on Sejda Web, against no task quota.
Editing existing PDF text, which PrivaTools does not offer.
A local desktop app, against a browser app you can self-host.
overview: Sejda offers online PDF tools, Sejda Web, and a desktop application, Sejda Desktop, for Windows, macOS and Linux, with a Chromebook route through the Linux environment. Its press page says Sejda started in 2010 as an open-source project; the Desktop licence agreement now states that the software is not open source.

Sejda Web uploads documents and processes them on Sejda's servers, and its tool pages say files are deleted automatically after two hours. Sejda Desktop processes files on your computer. Free use needs no signup and is limited per document, per task and per hour; a Week Pass, a Monthly plan and an Annual Desktop+Web plan lift those limits.

features.privatools: Free, with no passes or subscriptions.
features.competitor: Web Week Pass $5 for 7 days; Web Monthly $7.50 per user a month; Desktop+Web Annual $63 per user a year.

features.privatools: No hourly or daily task allowance; heavy jobs allow five runs a minute per IP.
features.competitor: Most free web tools: documents up to 200 pages or 50 MB, and 3 tasks per hour.

features.privatools: The same limits for everyone: 500 MB per request, about 250 MB per file on most pages.
features.competitor: No page or hourly limits, files up to 500 MB each, OCR up to 100 pages, up to 21 minutes per task.

features.privatools: Most PDF tools run on PrivaTools' server, or on your own if you self-host; there is no desktop app.
features.competitor: Sejda Desktop processes files on your computer rather than uploading them; Sejda Web uses its servers.

features.privatools: Removed after the response, with a sweep for leftovers older than ten minutes.
features.competitor: Tool pages say files are deleted automatically after 2 hours.

features.label: Source code
features.privatools: MIT-licensed and self-hostable.
features.competitor: The Desktop licence agreement says the software is not open source.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Any modern browser; installable as a web app.
features.competitor: Desktop for Mac (Intel and Apple silicon), Windows and Linux (.deb and .rpm), plus Chromebooks via Linux.

features.label: Editing
features.privatools: Edit PDF adds text, drawings, images and whiteout over the page.
features.competitor: Its tool menu lists editing existing PDF text.

sections.heading: How the free limits work
body: Sejda's free web tier suits occasional jobs but counts them. Most tools accept documents up to 200 pages or 50 MB, compress and deskew allow 100 MB, OCR and split by text stop at 10 pages, and every tool shares a limit of three tasks per hour. The free Desktop tier allows three tasks per day. A Week Pass lifts the web limits for seven days as a one-time charge that does not renew. Prices are in US dollars, with tax calculated at checkout.

PrivaTools has no task allowance to spend. Its limits are technical instead: 500 MB per upload request, about 250 MB per file on most tool pages, and per-IP rate limits on heavy jobs such as OCR and conversions. With nothing to buy, there is also no paid route past those limits on the public site.

sections.heading: Editing, splitting and scans
body: If you need to change words that are already in a PDF, Sejda lists existing-text editing; PrivaTools' Edit PDF places new text, shapes, images and whiteout on top of the page instead. Both split by bookmarks, by size and by text, and both straighten skewed scans and run OCR. Sejda also lists workflows, Bates numbering and a form tool that detects fields in a static PDF; PrivaTools has Bates numbering, a pipeline that chains PDF steps and a form creator where you place the fields yourself.

chooseCompetitor: You need to edit the existing text of a PDF, not only add to it.
You want a desktop app that processes documents on your computer, on Windows, macOS or Linux.
Three tasks an hour are enough, or a short paid pass fits an occasional project.
You want a form tool that finds the fields in a static PDF for you.
choosePrivaTools: You run more than a few jobs an hour and would rather not buy a pass.
You want the code open, and the option to run the service yourself.
Your files include images, audio or video as well as PDFs.
tradeoffs: Sejda's pages differ on retention: tool pages say two hours, while the home page and privacy policy say files are deleted after processing without giving a period.
Its licence agreement says Sejda Desktop contacts Sejda's servers to download OCR language data.
We did not benchmark either product's output.

name: PDF24
title: PrivaTools vs PDF24: free tools, EU servers and Creator

summary: Both are free. PDF24 pays for its online tools with advertising, processes uploads on servers in the EU and offers PDF24 Creator, a free Windows program that works offline and adds a virtual PDF printer. PrivaTools shows no advertising, runs some tools in your browser and the rest on its server, covers media and developer tasks as well as PDFs, and is open source and self-hostable.

overview: PDF24, from Geek Software GmbH, offers PDF24 Online Tools in the browser and PDF24 Creator, an application for Windows. Its FAQ says the tools are free for everyone, including companies, and are financed by discreet advertising on its websites. Its terms allow commercial use when document processing is not itself the core of your business, rule out automated scripts, and note that free provision is not guaranteed in future.

The online tools process files on PDF24's servers. Its FAQ says those servers are in EU data centres and that files are deleted automatically within one hour of processing, and a data processing agreement is available on request. PDF24 Creator works offline and keeps files on your PC, adding a virtual PDF printer, scanner and camera import, and screen capture.

sections.heading: Offline work on Windows
body: PDF24 Creator is the main difference. It installs on Windows, brings the PDF24 tools as an offline version, and adds features a website cannot: virtual PDF printers that turn anything you can print into a PDF, import from a scanner or camera, screen capture and an entry in File Explorer's context menu. Its manual also documents a command line for processing files in scripts.

PrivaTools has no desktop program. It runs in the browser on any operating system and installs as a web app; browser-only tools you have opened can keep working offline, but PDF conversions and OCR on the server need a connection. To keep everything on your own machine, you can run the Docker Compose project yourself.

sections.heading: Where uploads go
body: PDF24's online tools send files to its processing servers, which its FAQ places in EU data centres, and delete them within an hour; its privacy policy allows longer storage when processing takes longer than that. PrivaTools' server tools write uploads and results to temporary per-request files, remove them when the response has been sent, and sweep up leftovers older than ten minutes. If you need to control where processing happens, you can host PrivaTools on your own infrastructure.

You want uploads handled in EU data centres, with a data processing agreement on request.

You need image, audio, video or developer tools alongside PDF work.
tradeoffs: PDF24's FAQ places its servers in EU data centres, while its merge page says they are in Germany; both describe the same online tools.
Its Creator manual documents a setting that stops Creator using the online converter when no local converter is available; check it if files must stay on the PC.

sections.heading: Editing and document work
body: Foxit PDF Editor is a full editor. Its plans list editing text and images with paragraph reflow, OCR that makes scans searchable and editable, version comparison, fillable form creation, accessibility validation, PDF/A conversion and validation, and certificate signatures. PDF Editor+ adds Smart Redact and signature requests with tracking, and the product page lists 150 e-signature envelopes a year on Editor+. It integrates with Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box, OneDrive and Salesforce.

PrivaTools keeps these jobs separate and free: Compare PDF, Form Creator, OCR PDF, Redact PDF and the Accessibility Checker. It cannot edit existing text or apply certificate signatures, and its PDF to PDF/A tool labels a file as PDF/A-2b without validating it.

sections.heading: Online tools and AI
body: Foxit's free online converters run on its servers, and each sets its own size cap: PDF to Word and OCR take 15 MB, merging 20 MB per file and compression 150 MB. Its cloud AI features run on Microsoft Azure, with extracted data deleted within 24 hours, while Local AI in the desktop apps works without an internet connection.

PrivaTools' AI either runs in your browser with downloaded models, for summaries, translation, transcription and detecting personal data, or goes from your browser to a provider you choose, with your own key. There are no credits to buy.

name: LightPDF

PrivaTools does not resell AI. Chat with PDF, and the provider modes of Summarize, Translate and Transcribe, send requests from your browser straight to the provider whose key you add, and that provider bills you. Summarize, Translate and Transcribe can also run on-device models after a one-time download, with nothing sent to a provider.

Its help guide says processed files are stored temporarily and deleted regularly, the editor page gives 24 hours, the merge page says files are deleted after the changes are done, and ChatPDF keeps documents in encrypted cloud storage until you delete them. The free plan includes cloud storage of five files for a year.

PrivaTools has no cloud storage. Server tools write inputs and results to temporary per-request files that are removed after the response, with a background sweep for leftovers older than ten minutes; the copies that remain are the ones you download.

name: Stirling PDF
title: PrivaTools vs Stirling PDF: two self-hostable toolkits
description: Stirling PDF is an open-core PDF editor with desktop apps and paid Team plans; PrivaTools is an MIT-licensed web toolbox. Plans, licences and hosting compared.
summary: Both can run on your own server. Stirling PDF is a PDF-focused editor that also ships desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux, and sells Team and Enterprise licences for larger self-hosted installations. PrivaTools covers PDFs plus images, audio, video and developer utilities in one web app under the MIT licence, with no paid tier.
highlights: Open-core licensing with paid tiers, against MIT with no paid tier.
Desktop apps with a local mode, against a browser app you install as a PWA.
Single sign-on and audit logs on paid plans, which PrivaTools does not offer.
overview: Stirling PDF describes itself as open-core: its repository is MIT-licensed except for listed directories that carry a proprietary Stirling PDF User License, and production use of that proprietary code needs a valid licence. It offers desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux, self-hosting with Docker, Kubernetes or a Java .jar, and a hosted version at stirling.com/app.

Its pricing page lists a Free plan at $0 a month, a Team plan at $99 a month with 100 users included, an Enterprise plan on custom terms, and a PDF Processor billed at 1 cent per credit. Its documentation adds that a Team licence covers one installation, and that the licence tier decides which features, such as single sign-on, SAML and audit logs, are unlocked.

sections.heading: Licences and what you pay for
body: Stirling PDF's free tier suits individuals and small groups: its documentation limits free self-hosted installations to five users and says a Team licence, at $99 a month, covers one installation with 100 users. Enterprise adds SAML sign-in, audit logs, SCIM provisioning and air-gapped deployment. Because proprietary directories sit inside an otherwise MIT repository, check which features your deployment uses before assuming all of it is freely licensed.

PrivaTools has no licence tiers. The same MIT-licensed code runs the public site and any copy you host, and nothing is unlocked by payment. The trade-off is that PrivaTools has no organisation features: accounts exist to issue developer API keys, not to manage teams.

sections.heading: Running it yourself
body: Stirling documents Docker, Kubernetes with Helm, bare-metal .jar installs and managed desktop fleets, where IT pre-configures desktop installs through device-management tools. Its automation includes a REST API, pipelines, folder scanning and an MCP server for AI assistants, and its 2.14 desktop release added signing with USB tokens and smart cards. PrivaTools ships as a Docker Compose project whose heavy tools rely on bundled engines such as LibreOffice, Tesseract and FFmpeg, so plan for their CPU and memory use.
On the public PrivaTools site you run nothing: browser-only tools keep their input on the device, and server tools upload to temporary storage that is cleaned after the response.

Your organisation needs single sign-on, audit logs or user management and can budget for a licence.
You want to automate PDF work with its pipelines, folder scanning or REST API on your own server.
You need certificate signing from a USB token or smart card on the desktop.
choosePrivaTools: You want every feature under one permissive licence, with no seat count to track.
Your work mixes PDFs with images, audio, video, archives and developer utilities.
You want AI features that run on your device or with your own provider key.
You would like to try a public site first and self-host later with the same tools.

Self-hosting either product makes you responsible for updates, backups, logs and capacity, and for how the copy you run handles files.

sections.heading: Forms, annotations and signatures

Its help centre also notes that the free online editor can modify only text that was added in PDFescape.

PrivaTools covers the same ground with separate free tools. Fill Form enters values into existing fields; Form Creator adds text, checkbox, radio, dropdown, list and signature fields; Annotate PDF adds highlights, underlines and sticky notes; Redact PDF removes the content under each box; and OCR PDF makes scans searchable. Its signatures are images placed on the page, not certificate-based signatures.

sections.heading: What happens to your documents

features.competitor: Its web-based tools take files up to 100 MB and 500 pages.

features.label: Where files are processed
features.privatools: In the browser tab for local tools, or on PrivaTools' server for conversions, with nothing to install.
features.competitor: Downloadable software on your own computers, plus cloud services reached over the internet.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed; an optional account issues API keys.
features.competitor: An active Nitro subscription or licence is required to use the product.

features.label: Source code
features.privatools: MIT-licensed and self-hostable.
features.competitor: Proprietary: Nitro remains the sole owner of its software and IP.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Any modern browser; installable as a web app.
features.competitor: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), macOS 10.14 or later, and iOS.

features.label: Editing existing text
features.privatools: Edit PDF adds text, drawings, images and whiteout over the page.
features.competitor: Edits text within a paragraph and reflows it inside the text box as you type.

sections.heading: Editing depth
body: Nitro is a full desktop editor. Its Windows guide describes editing existing paragraphs with text reflow, and its plans include OCR that turns scans into editable, searchable PDFs, conversion to Word, Excel and PowerPoint, and batch processing for conversion, printing and OCR. Its AI Document Assistant runs on Azure OpenAI, and Nitro says documents are deleted once the task is complete.

PrivaTools approaches the same jobs as separate tools. Edit PDF draws new content over the page rather than changing existing text; OCR PDF adds a searchable text layer with a server or browser engine; PDF to Word extracts text line by line into an editable draft without rebuilding paragraphs or tables. For a document you revise every day, a desktop editor such as Nitro does more.

sections.heading: Signatures and teams
body: Nitro Sign is sold as its own plans, and the Mac app can send documents for signature with Nitro Sign or DocuSign. Single sign-on for the PDF apps is listed on the Plus plan. PrivaTools has no signature-request workflow: Sign PDF and E-Sign PDF place a visible signature image that you add yourself, and nothing in the file records who signed or whether it changed afterwards.

chooseCompetitor: You edit existing text, images and forms in PDFs every day and want a desktop app.
You need scans made searchable and editable, with batch OCR or conversion.
Your team sends documents for signature and tracks them, or needs single sign-on.
choosePrivaTools: You need a quick task done without installing software or starting a trial.
You work on Linux or another system Nitro's apps do not cover, using only a browser.
You want image, audio, video and developer tools alongside PDFs, with open code.
tradeoffs: Nitro's own pages differ on some details, such as the iOS version it needs and where its data centres are; check the documentation for your platform before buying.
Placing a signature image and running a signature-request service are different jobs; compare them separately.
We did not benchmark editing accuracy, OCR quality or speed.

name: TinyWow
title: PrivaTools vs TinyWow: free tools, plans and file handling
description: TinyWow offers free PDF, image, video and AI writing tools, with paid plans that list no ads; PrivaTools has no ads and is open source. Plans and data compared.
summary: TinyWow is a broad free toolbox, now part of Jenni AI, covering PDF, image, video, file conversion and AI writing tasks without registration. Its pricing page also sells optional plans whose features include no ads, faster processing and no captcha. PrivaTools covers PDFs, images, audio, video and developer data with no paid tier, no advertising and open code, but it has no AI writing or downloading tools.
highlights: AI writing and object-removal tools, which PrivaTools does not offer.
Paid plans that list no ads or captchas, against no ads and no paid tier.
Uploads deleted within an hour on US servers, against cleanup after each response.
overview: TinyWow offers online tools for PDFs, images, video, file conversion and AI writing, and its terms say the site does not currently require registration or fees. Its about page says it joined forces with Jenni.ai in 2025, and its footer describes it as a Jenni AI company. Processing happens on its servers, which its privacy policy says are hosted in the United States.

Its pricing page says the tools are free to use without registration and lists optional paid plans, shown to us in Indian rupees, whose features include no ads, faster processing, no captcha and early access to new tools. Its privacy policy says uploaded files are deleted an hour after processing, and that analytics and third-party tracking are used to personalise the ads it serves.

features.label: Price
features.privatools: Free, with no paid tier.
features.competitor: Free without registration; optional monthly or yearly plans list no ads, faster processing and no captcha.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed for any tool.
features.competitor: No registration or fees currently required; subscriptions are managed in an account.

features.label: Where files are processed
features.privatools: Developer and text tools run in your browser; file conversions run on PrivaTools' server in temporary storage.
features.competitor: On its servers, hosted in the United States.

features.label: Retention
features.privatools: Deleted by response cleanup, with a background sweep for anything older than ten minutes.
features.competitor: The privacy policy says uploaded files are deleted one hour after processing.

features.label: Ads and tracking
features.privatools: No ad networks; Google Analytics is on by default with an off switch on the Privacy page.
features.competitor: Analytics and third-party tracking are used to personalise the ads it serves.

features.label: Source code
features.privatools: MIT-licensed and self-hostable.
features.competitor: The terms say the underlying software is the property of TinyWow and its partners.

features.label: Tool range
features.privatools: PDF, image, audio, video, archive and developer tools, with on-device or own-key AI.
features.competitor: Tools for PDFs, images, video, AI writing and file conversion.

sections.heading: Two different kinds of breadth
body: Both toolboxes are broad, in different directions. TinyWow's catalogue includes AI writing tools such as an AI humanizer, a PDF translator, e-signing, audio to text, background removal, a TikTok video downloader and a photo clean-up tool that removes unwanted objects from images. PrivaTools has no text generators or downloaders; its breadth is in file operations such as PDF editing and conversion, OCR, audio and video conversion, archives and developer formats, many of which run entirely in the browser.

sections.heading: How files are handled
body: TinyWow processes uploads on servers in the United States. Its privacy policy, last revised in March 2023, says files are deleted one hour after processing; its tool pages say one hour after upload, and its terms say 15 minutes after processing. The privacy policy also says TinyWow does not sell information about its users or their files.

PrivaTools labels each tool before it runs: browser tools keep the input on the device, and server tools write it to temporary per-request storage that is cleaned after the response. PrivaTools uses Google Analytics by default for page views and tool-run events, which never include file names or contents, and you can switch it off on the Privacy page.

chooseCompetitor: You want AI writing or humanizing tools next to your file tools.
You need its video downloader or its tool for removing objects from photos.
You are happy with a free tier supported by ads, or want its paid plan for faster processing.
choosePrivaTools: You want tools without ads, captchas or a paid plan.
You want some tasks to stay in your browser, with a clear label on every tool that does not.
You want to read the code or run the service on your own server.
tradeoffs: TinyWow's own pages disagree on retention and on ads: its terms call the site ad-free, its privacy policy describes personalised ads, and its pricing page lists no ads as a paid feature.
Its pricing page showed rupee and dollar prices side by side when we checked; confirm the currency at checkout.
We did not benchmark output quality for either toolbox.

name: ihatepdf.cv
title: PrivaTools vs ihatepdf.cv: browser-only PDF tools compared
description: ihatepdf.cv runs its PDF tools in the browser and sends chat text to Google Gemini; PrivaTools mixes browser and server tools under an MIT licence.
summary: Both sites let you work without an account. ihatepdf.cv says its PDF tools run in the browser with WebAssembly, is free without ads and is funded by donations; its terms say the code is not open source. PrivaTools runs some tools in the browser and others on its server, covers images, media and developer tasks too, and publishes its code under the MIT licence.
highlights: Browser-first PDF tools, against a mix of browser and disclosed server tools.
Proprietary code, against an MIT-licensed, self-hostable project.
PDF chat through Google Gemini, against a choice of AI providers.
overview: ihatepdf.cv is a free collection of PDF and document tools that, by its own description, run in the web browser: its merge page says processing uses WebAssembly and files do not leave the device. Its about page names three tools that involve another party by design: Chat with PDF, P2P Share and a collaborative whiteboard.

The site says it has no ads, no paid tier and no account, and is kept running by voluntary donations. It uses Microsoft Clarity to understand how pages are used, and its terms state that the software is not open source and that no licence to reuse it is granted.

features.label: Price
features.privatools: Free to use, with no paid tier and no advertising.
features.competitor: Free, with no ads or paid tier; funded by voluntary donations.

features.label: File limits
features.privatools: 500 MB per server request, about 250 MB per file on most pages; browser tools depend on your device.
features.competitor: No server limit for merging; typically up to 150 MB across all files on a desktop, set by device memory.

features.label: Where files are processed
features.privatools: Each tool states whether it runs in your browser or uploads for temporary server processing.
features.competitor: In the browser with WebAssembly; three tools involve another party by design.

features.label: AI chat
features.privatools: Extracted text goes from your browser to your chosen provider: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, Together AI or a local server.
features.competitor: Chat with PDF sends the extracted text to Google's Gemini API, using a key you supply.

features.label: Account
features.privatools: Not needed; an optional account issues API keys.
features.competitor: No account or email required.

features.label: Source code
features.privatools: MIT-licensed and self-hostable.
features.competitor: Its terms say it is not open source and grant no licence to reuse it.

features.label: Platforms
features.privatools: Browser app, installable as a PWA; previously opened browser tools can work offline.
features.competitor: Its homepage says the site works offline after the first page load.

features.label: Analytics
features.privatools: Google Analytics on by default, with an off switch on the Privacy page; no file names or contents.
features.competitor: Microsoft Clarity is used to understand how pages are used.

sections.heading: What local processing covers
body: ihatepdf.cv's merge page says files never leave the device because processing runs in WebAssembly, and it ties capacity to memory: typically 20 to 50 files, or about 150 MB in total, on a desktop browser. Its pages are not fully consistent about AI summaries: the homepage calls Summarize PDF on-device, while the tool's own page says extracted text is sent to an AI service. Read the page for the exact tool before sending anything sensitive.

PrivaTools labels every tool. Developer utilities, text tools and several AI tools run in the browser; PDF conversions, the default OCR engine and media work run on the server, where inputs sit in temporary per-request storage and are cleaned after the response.

sections.heading: Asking questions about a PDF
body: Both products extract the PDF's text in the browser before a chat. ihatepdf.cv then sends that text to Google Gemini with a key you supply, and keeps the key in your browser only if you choose to save it. PrivaTools' Chat with PDF sends the text, your question and recent messages straight from the browser to the provider you select, without routing them through PrivaTools. Either way, the provider's own terms and charges apply.

chooseCompetitor: You want PDF tools that its pages describe as running entirely in the browser.
You already use a Gemini API key and want to chat with a PDF using it.
You need its India-specific document tools, such as its GST invoice and POS billing tools.
choosePrivaTools: You want to read, audit or self-host the code that processes your files.
Your tasks go beyond PDFs to images, audio, video, archives and developer data.
You want a choice of AI providers, or a server or browser engine for OCR.
tradeoffs: A file that stays in the browser can still have its text sent elsewhere: on both sites, chat features send extracted text to an AI provider.
Browser processing is bound by device memory; ihatepdf.cv's own merge figures vary by device, while PrivaTools' server tools have fixed request limits instead.
Neither product's output quality or speed was benchmarked for this page.
